title: Economic Viability of Integrated CO2 Capture and Conversion

metadata.authors: Y. Kim; M. Namdari; A. M. L. Jewlal; Y. Chen; D. J. D. Pimlott; M. Stolar; C. P. Berlinguette

source_summary: Integrating a bicarbonate electrolyzer with a CO₂ capture unit enables efficient, electrochemical CO₂ release and conversion to valuable products at a commercially viable cost, despite challenges in aligning optimal pH conditions for both processes.
abstract: The capture of CO<inf>2</inf> using alkaline solutions requires significant thermal energy to release CO<inf>2</inf> from a (bi)carbonate-enriched solution. This release of CO<inf>2</inf> can instead be performed electrochemically with a “bicarbonate electrolyzer”. The bicarbonate electrolyzer forms acid equivalents to convert a (bi)carbonate-enriched eluent from a CO<inf>2</inf> capture unit into CO<inf>2</inf> and, in turn, an upgraded carbon product such as CO and ethylene. There exists a tension for this closed-loop cycle to be put into practice: a smaller CO<inf>2</inf> capture unit is required when using a more caustic CO<inf>2</inf> capture solution, yet the electrolyzer works more effectively at a lower pH. Here, we elaborate on three different methods to align different pH regimes to couple air capture to CO<inf>2</inf> electrolysis. We also use a mass-balance model to assess the commercial viability of a reactive carbon capture system that integrates the CO<inf>2</inf> capture unit with a bicarbonate electrolyzer to show a levelized CO breakeven price below $1 kg<inf>CO</inf>-1. These economics, coupled with the other practical advantages of providing an electrolyzer with a liquid feedstock, present a compelling case for reactive carbon capture. © 2024 American Chemical Society.
